content: Uterine carcinosarcomas are rare malignancies, with approximately 35% of cases presenting with disease that has already spread beyond the uterus at the time of diagnosis. Women with advanced stages of this cancer generally have poor survival outcomes, with a high likelihood of recurrence in the upper abdomen and distant metastatic sites. The purpose of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of adjuvant radiotherapy and/or systemic chemotherapy in the treatment of uterine carcinosarcoma. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to November 2012. Additional sources, such as clinical trial registries, conference abstracts, reference lists of relevant studies, and consultations with field experts, were also utilized. The analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared adjuvant radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy in women diagnosed with uterine carcinosarcoma. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. Hazard ratios (HRs) for overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), as well as risk ratios (RRs) for adverse events, were calculated and pooled using random-effects meta-analyses. Three trials, involving a total of 579 women, met the inclusion criteria. All participants were evaluated at the conclusion of the trials. Two of these trials, which included 373 women with stage III to IV persistent or recurrent disease, demonstrated that combination chemotherapy significantly reduced the risk of death and disease progression compared to single-agent ifosfamide. After adjusting for performance status, the hazard ratio for overall survival (OS) was 0.75 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.60 to 0.94), and for progression-free survival (PFS), it was 0.72 (95% CI: 0.58 to 0.90). However, women in the combination therapy group experienced significantly higher rates of nausea and vomiting compared to those receiving ifosfamide alone (RR = 3.53, 95% CI: 1.33 to 9.37). No other adverse events showed statistically significant differences between the groups. In a separate trial, no statistically significant differences were observed in the risk of death or disease progression between women treated with whole-body irradiation and those receiving chemotherapy, after adjusting for age and FIGO stage. The hazard ratio for overall survival was 0.71 (95% CI: 0.48 to 1.05), and for progression-free survival, it was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.53 to 1.18). However, significantly fewer women in the whole-body irradiation group experienced hematological toxicities compared to the chemotherapy group (RR = 0.02, 95% CI: 0.00 to 0.16). Additionally, all nine cases of neuropathy reported in this trial occurred in the chemotherapy group. In conclusion, for women with advanced-stage metastatic or recurrent uterine carcinosarcoma, adjuvant combination chemotherapy, particularly with ifosfamide and paclitaxel, is associated with a lower risk of death compared to ifosfamide alone. However, abdominal radiotherapy does not appear to improve survival outcomes.
